OFFICE MEMORANDUM Sub: Seeking comments/ views/ suggestions from Stakeholders on Recruitment Rules for Group A posts in PCIM&H- reg.

The undersigned is directed to say that as per DoPT’s O.M. No. AB- 14017/61/2008-Estt(RR) dated 13.10.2015, the framing/ Amendment of Recruitment Rules are to be uploaded on the website of respective Ministries/ Departments for 30 days inviting comments from the stakeholders.

2. Accordingly Draft RRs. for Group A posts in PCIM&H are forwarded (hard copy as well as soft copy) to Web Manager with request :-

(A) To upload the draft Recruitment Rules for the Group ‘A’ posts in Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy (PCIM&H) alongwith the above OM on the oﬃcial website of Ministry of Ayush under the Title 'What's New" for 30 days for getting inputs, if any, from the stakeholders.

(B) To provide a link of feedback at the site of "What's New" itself for stakeholders so that they may give feedbacks/suggestions inserting comments thereto, and

(C) To insert a para just below the subject to the eﬀect, " All the stakeholders are, therefore, requested to peruse the draft RRs and give their inputs either at the the link of Feedback or through email to Director PCIM&H [e-mail: dir.pcimh-ayush@gov.in] in a tabular form (in word ﬁle) by speciﬁcally indicating the para number, original content and the change suggested w.r.t., the original contents within a period of 30 Days from the date of its uploading on the website."

Encl.: As above

(Madan Lal Meena) Under Secretary to the Government of India

To

1. Web Manager, MoA, NBCC Building, Kidwai Nagar for taking action as mentioned above. A-12018/2/2023-LP I/88763/2025

2. Director, PCIM&H, with request to get the RRs. uploaded on the web-site of PCIM&H on the above lines. text:
No. 0-19013/24/2022-SUS Government of India Ministry of Ayush Siddha & Unani Section Ayush Bhawan, B-Block, GPO Complex, WJA, New Delhi-i 10023 Dated: 13th October, 2026 VACANCY CIRCULAR Subject: Filling up the post of Director General, Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine, New Delhi.

The undersigned is directed to say that Ministry of Ayush proposes to fill up the post of Director General, Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine (CCRUM), New Delhi, an Autonomous Body under the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India. The post is proposed to be filled up on deputation basis, including short term contract basis for a period not exceeding 5 years. The details regarding eligibility conditions for the post etc. are given in Annex-I.

2. The application, in the prescribed proforma, complete in all respects, should reach through proper channel to Shri Arjun Kumar, Under Secretary, Ministry of Ayush, Government of India, Ayush Bhawan, B-Block, GPO Complex, 1NA, New Delhi-110023, within 60 days from the date of publication of the advertisement for the said post of DG, CCRUM, in the Employment News/Rozgar Samachar. The format for the application is given at Annex-Il.

Details are also available on the websites of this Ministry (www.ayush.gov.in ) and CCRUM's website (https://ccrum.ayush.gov.in/).

3. This issues with the approval of Competent Authority. End: As above. (Arjun Kumar) Under Secretary to the Government of India To: All Ministries/Departments/Chief Secretaries to State/UT Governments (for wider circulation of the vacancy) Copy to:

3. इच्छुक अभ्यधथणयों को वर्वधधर्वत भरे हुए आर्वेदन-पत्र (जो आरएर्वी की र्वेबसाइट पर उपलब्ध है) के साथ शैक्षखर्क योग्यता, अनुभर्व प्रमार्-पत्र, आयु प्रमार्-पत्र तथा अन्य संबंधधत दस्तार्वेजों की स्र्वप्रमाखर्त प्रनतयाँ लेकर र्वॉक-इन-इंटरव्यू में उपश्स्थत होना होगा। आर्वेदन-पत्र एर्वं संबंधधत दस्तार्वेज साक्षात्कार के ददन ननधाणररत स्थल पर जमा ककए जाएंगे।

4. अभ्यधथणयों को सत्यापन हेतु साक्षात्कार के समय सभी मूल दस्तार्वेज भी साथ लाने होंगे। दटप्पखर्याँ :

1. आयु सीमा का ननधाणरर् वर्वज्ञापन की नतधथ के अनुसार ककया जाएगा।

2. अभ्यधथणयों की पात्रता का ननधाणरर् ननधाणररत अननर्वायण योग्यता के आधार पर ककया जाएगा।

3. साक्षात्कार में सश्म्मललत होने हेतु ककसी प्रकार का यात्रा भत्ता/दैननक भत्ता (TA/DA) देय नहीं होगा।

4. ननदेशक, राष्ट्रीय आयुर्वेद वर्वद्यापीठ (RAV) को त्रबना कोई कारर् बताए ककसी भी आर्वेदन को स्र्वीकार अथर्वा अस्र्वीकार करने तथा साक्षात्कार को स्थधगत अथर्वा ननरस्त करने का अधधकार सुरक्षक्षत रहेगा।

5. अभ्यथी आगे की अद्यतन जानकारी के ललए समय-समय पर राष्ट्रीय आयुर्वेद वर्वद्यापीठ (RAV) की र्वेबसाइट तथा आयुष मंत्रालय की र्वेबसाइट का अर्वलोकन करते रहें।

title: Ministry of Ayush, Government of India — NIT
text:
MINISTRY OF AYUSH

Expression of Interest (EOI) For Selection of CPSU for Preparation of Detailed Project Report (DPR) for Establishing three AIIA Institutes and Upgradation of traditional medicine infrastructure across the WHO- GTMC Centre at Jamnagar

Brief details of the tender Tender No. NIT- 01/2026/MoA Name of work Preparation of DPR including preliminary estimates for

i. Establishing three AIIA Institutes in 3 different States / UTs

ii. Upgradation of traditional medicine infrastructure across the WHO-GTMC Centre at Jamnagar

Time for completion of work 4 weeks (From the date of award of assignment) Tender invitation date 07.09.2026 Amount of Earnest Money Deposit Rs.1, 20, 000/- (Rs. One lakh Twenty Thousands Only) Last date of Online submission 21.09.2026 Date & time of opening of financial bids 22.09.2026

EXPRESSION OF INTEREST The Ministry of Ayush invites proposals from eligible CPSUs for the preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPR) for the following projects:

i. Establishment of Three All India Institute of Ayurveda in 3 different States/UTs of the country (3 separate DPRs)

ii. Upgradation of traditional medicine infrastructure across the WHO-GTMC Centre at Jamnagar The DPRs must be compliant with the General Financial Rules (GFR) and of guidelines of the Department of Expenditure Ministry of Finance, Government of India.

1. PROJECT PROPOSALS IN BRIEF During the presentation of the Union Budget 2026–27 on 1st February, 2026, the Hon’ble Finance Minister announced:

i. Establishment of three new All India Institutes of Ayurveda (AIIAs)

ii. Upgradation of the WHO-GTMC Centre at Jamnagar.

In pursuance of the above, following project proposals have been formulated:-

A. Establishment of 3 AIIA Institutes Ministry has setup a benchmark at tertiary level healthcare through its National Institutes like All India Institute of Ayurveda (New Delhi), ITRA (Jamnagar), National Institute of Ayurveda (Jaipur), National Institute of Unani Medicine (Bangalore), National Institute of Siddha (Chennai), National Institute of Homeopathy (Kolkata) etc. Besides providing advanced healthcare and creating a pool of well-trained human resource, these institutes have been majorly contributing in drug development, standardization and scientific validation of medicines and treatment protocols, translational research, public health related R&D and education. The institutes have also pioneered in setting up strong collaborations internationally.

title: Ministry of Ayush, Government of India — NIT
text:
and creating a pool of well-trained human resource, these institutes have been majorly contributing in drug development, standardization and scientific validation of medicines and treatment protocols, translational research, public health related R&D and education. The institutes have also pioneered in setting up strong collaborations internationally.

Keeping in view the encouraging experience with the AIIA and other National institutes, setting up new AIIA like institutes in different traditional systems of medicine in different regions of the country has been proposed as a key initiative of Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.

The Ministry is in the process of finalizing the locations for the 3 AIIA projects by Challenge Method. In this regard, the different States has been requested to submit their Bid proposals for evaluation. The Bids from eligible states have been received and the

evaluation of the Bids are under process. The evaluation exercise and finalization of the sites for the 3 AIIA institutes is expected by 15th September, 2026. Scope of AIIA Project:

The Ministry has carried out a detailed exercise to standardize the level of academic activities, physical infrastructure (Buildings, medical equipment) and Faculty and other human resource to be provisioned for in each new institute proposed to be set up. The standardization has been done keeping in view the imperative that there has to be emphasis on higher education and research. The requirement of hospital beds, faculty, paramedics and built-up spaces has been assessed keeping in view the NCISM (MSR guidelines). However, for determining the area requirement for the private/ semiprivate wards in the hospitals and in the academic block the experience gained/ difficulties and constraints experienced in AIIA, Sarita Vihar, AIIA Goa and NIA Panchkula has also been taken into consideration. For hostels and residential accommodations, CPWD norms have been followed.

title: Ministry of Ayush, Government of India — NIT
text:
for the private/ semiprivate wards in the hospitals and in the academic block the experience gained/ difficulties and constraints experienced in AIIA, Sarita Vihar, AIIA Goa and NIA Panchkula has also been taken into consideration. For hostels and residential accommodations, CPWD norms have been followed.

Based on the above considerations, the following key standards are envisaged in each AIIA: Academic Activities  UG course - 100 Seats  Departments - 15  PG courses - 90 Seats  Ph. D - 45 Seats  Nursing / Paramedical (Short upskilling courses)- 120 Seats Faculty required (144)  Professor - 29  Additional Professor - 22  Associate Professor - 36  Assistant Professor - 57 Hospital infrastructure  350 Bed hospital  Surgical and non-Surgical units  06 Modular OTs  45 OPD clinics  Speciality Clinic – 10 No  Diagnostic services  Yoga and Meditation Hall  Panchakarma therapy block

Hostel Facilities Special provision for foreigner students

In order to smoothly run the above activities / services, the Ministry has estimated the built up area requirements for different buildings, proposed to be built at each AIIA Campus, as below:- S. No. Building Description Area (Sqm) 1 Hospital Block (350 beds) (G+6) 34628 2 Academic Block (G+8) 19294 3 Hostels Block(G+8) 23565 4 Residential Block (G+8+ 31709 5 Auditorium Block 2180 6 Pharmacy Block (G+1) 2394 7 Sub Station / Service Block 812 8 GYM, Yoga & Swimming Pool 1840 9 Other Building 1840 10 Clinical Unit (G+1) 1625 Total built up area 119887 11 Herbal Garden 4000

All buildings are majorly planned to be multi storied building. The total ground coverage is expected to be 22,000 Sq M, for each AIIA.

B. Upgradation of traditional medicine infrastructure across the WHO-GTMC Centre at Jamnagar Under the project, the Ministry envisages to set up with following for facilities:

i. Setting up of a Global Traditional Medicine Village (GTMV) with following key components  Medicinal Plant Business Centre  Global Traditional Medicine Museum  Ayush Incubation Centre

 State-of-the-art Yoga Centre  Herbal Garden

ii. Setting up of a state-of-the-Art advanced care 500 Bed speciality Ayurveda Hospital (Capitalizing on the presence of the ITRA at Jamnagar)

The total ground coverage is expected to be 27305 Sq M

2. Scope of the Work under present Consultancy Tender The scope of work shall involve preparation of the DPRs for the 3 AIIA projects and the project for “Upgradation of traditional medicine infrastructure across the WHO-GTMC Centre at Jamnagar”. Each DPR preparation will encompass the following:- Preparation of Detailed Project Report (DPR) with due care and accuracy, using latest technological tools collecting all relevant ground information, including consultation with the field units, wherever applicable. The DPR will involve carrying out of the following activities and preparation of the following details / information as mentioned below:

i. Concept plan/ preliminary drawings and their acceptance - This shall indicate the details of Concept plan/ preliminary drawings prepared and their approval by the requisitioning authority;

ii. Pre-requisite for DPR: Site Survey and soil investigation. The Soil investigation activity will require drilling of boreholes as below:

a. For each AIIA Institute project Minimum 5 boreholes (one at each of 4 corners and one in the centre) in every 4000 square meter area, where construction is envisaged. The total ground coverage is expected to be 22000 square metre. Thus, in all 25 boreholes would be required to be drilled in area, where construction is envisaged. The selected agency should judiciously plan the location of the boreholes.

3. Eligibility Criteria 3.1 As per Rule 133 (3), General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, Govt. of India following CPSUs will be eligible to participate in the bid: Any Public Sector Undertaking set up by the Central Government to carry out civil or electrical works Or Notified by the Ministry or Urban Development (MoUD), Government of India for such purpose after evaluating their financial strength and technical competence.

3.2 The CPSUs must not be blacklisted or debarred by any Govt. and no work awarded to CPSUs should have been terminated during the last three years on the ground of unsatisfactory performance, at the time of submission of bid. 3(A) Relevant Experience Minimum of ten years’ experience in DPR preparation / execution of work involving construction of multi-storeyed Hospital buildings/ office buildings / Institutional Buildings/ Commercial buildings. Details should be furnished in Annexure-I, in support of the eligibility.

4. Earnest Money Deposit: Each bid should be accompanied by an Earnest Money Deposit of Rs.1.20 Lakhs (Rupees one lakh and twenty thousand only). Earnest Money should be deposited along with the Technical bid by means of Bank Guarantee (in the respective format enclosed as Annexure II) drawn in favour of the Pay and Accounts Officer, Ministry of Ayush, Govt. of India, payable at Delhi .The Earnest Money Deposit shall have to be valid for at least six months beyond the last date of submission of the bid. The bids not accompanied by Earnest Money or Earnest Money being in deviation from above, shall be summarily rejected. No interest shall be payable by the Employer for the sum deposited as EMD.

4.1 Earnest Money will be returned to all unsuccessful PSUs without interest after completion of the tender process. 4.2 The Earnest Money shall be liable for forfeiture in the following events:

i. If the bid is withdrawn during the validity period or any extended validity period agreed to by the bidder.

ii. If the bid is varied or modified in a manner not acceptable to the employer after opening of the bid during the validity period or any extension thereof.

iii. If the bidder tries to influence the evaluation process.

Performance Security Deposit: 5.1 Successful CPSUs shall, within 07 days from the date of conveying acceptance of the tender in his favour in writing, have to deposit sum equal to five per cent of the total Consultancy fee for the preparation of DPRs as security for the fulfilment of the contract, in the form of a Bank Guarantee (in the prescribed format in Annexure IV) drawn in favour of the Pay & Accounts Officer, Ministry of Ayush, Govt. of India, payable at Delhi.

5.2 The Performance Security Deposit must remain valid for a minimum period of ninety days beyond the stipulated completion date of this consultancy contract.

6. Documents / details to be submitted in the offer: The bidder is required to furnish the following details / documents duly signed and stamped on each page by the authorized signatory of the bidder: -

i. Technical Details about the CPSU and other relevant information in the formats prescribed at Annexure I to IV including documents in the details provided therein.

ii. Copy of Certificates for GST Registration and copy of PAN.

iii. A certificate from the Chairman / Company Secretary of the PSU certifying the details of the signatory authority and attestation of such authority’s signature or Power of Attorney in favor of the signatory authority for the purpose of signing bid documents. Note:

8. Time Frame: All four DPRs, complete all respects, are required to be submitted within 4 weeks after the work is assigned to the successful CPSU.

9. Payment Terms The full consultancy fee in reference to each DPR would be payable on successful completion of the assignment, i.e., final preparation of the DPR and its acceptance by the Ministry of Ayush.

(Indian Standard Time) on 21.09.2026 Ministry of Ayush, at its discretion, may extend the deadline for the submission of the proposals prior to the date and time of last date of submission of Bids, as it may deem appropriate.

The Financial proposal shall not include any conditions to it and any such conditional financial proposal shall be rejected summarily.

Guidelines and procedure for engagement of Consultants and Young Professionals in the Ministry of Avush (Applicable w.e.f. 01 April 2026) The engagement of non-officials as consultant and Young Professional on contract basis in the Ministry of Ayush shall henceforth be regulated as per the following guidelines and process:

I. GENERAL

• I The purpose of these guidelines is to defme the broad procedures for selection, contracting and monitoring of consultants and Young Professional engaged by Ministry of Ayush. 1.2 The engagement of consultants and Young Professionals shall be for specific purpose (s) and for specified duration as per procedure prescribed here under. However, following may be the main reasons for engagement: -

(a) The absence of required expertise in house, or

(b) The need for economy and efficiency, or

(c) The need to have highly qualified experts for providing the specific services. 1.3 The consultants and Young Professionals would be appointed to undertake mainly the following work:

i. Work related with implementation of the schemes of the Ministry of Ayush, organizing Seminars/Conferences, preparation of agenda, briefs, speeches, minutes, Annual Report, Preparation of Annual Plan, Budget and accounts, court cases/legal matters, technical consultancy etc. under the active supervision of Programme Division.

ii. The Consultants and Young Professionals would provide secretarial services, office support in order to ensure a high level of efficiency and effectiveness of office administration.

IV. Ayush Hospitals/Day Care Centres located in X (Tier -I) cities: 20% higher than rates for Z (Tier-III) cities. V. Y (Tier-II) rates also apply to Ayush Hospitals/Day Care Centres in the North-East region and Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. VI. Package rates for Shalya, Shalakya and Prasuti Tantra & Stree Roga procedures of Ayurveda (Annexure-2) pertain to general wards. For semi -private wards, rates shall increase by 5%; for private wards, by 10% on the admissible claim amount (appli cable only for treatments requiring admission). If treatment provided on OPD/day care basis, rates will be considered for general wards only irrespective of ward entitlement.

VII. Separate pre and post-procedure costs are not applicable, as they have been incorporated into the revised procedure rates. VIII. The forwarding letter containing the applications for nomination should be addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Ayush, and shall reach this Ministry within 45 days from the date of issuance of this letter, except in the case of the North Eastern States. Chandrasura (Lepidium sativum L.) is a time-honoured medicinal and nutritional plant, revered across Ayurveda, Siddha, , Unani and Homeopathy traditions for its remarkable healing properties. This dossier unveils the science and tradition behind this safe yet powerful seed.

II CHANDRASURA SAFETY DOSSIER Prologue Lepidium sativum Linn., commonly known as Chandrasura, Garden cress, or Asaliyo, is an important medicinal and nutritional plant recognized in Ayush systems i.e. Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Homoeopathy. Classical texts also mentioned its use in Paushtika yoga (nutritive formulations) and as a Bala vardhaka (strength-promoting agent). It is valued for its diverse therapeutic applications, particularly its traditional use in improving digestion, acting as a galactagogue, enhancing hematinic status, supporting respiratory health, and promoting general strength and immunity. The seeds are rich in bioactive constituents, including glucosinolates, flavonoids, alkaloids, and fatty acids, as well as providing a natural source of iron, calcium, and folic acid, thereby important for nutraceutical and pharmaceutical applications. In recent years, Chandrasura has gained increasing attention for its pharmacological potential, with research highlighting its anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antidiabetic, hepatoprotective, bone-strengthening, and wound-healing properties.

Beyond its medicinal relevance, L. sativum has garnered recognition in contemporary nutrition science as a nutraceutical and functional food. Its sprouts and microgreens, owing to their high density of vitamins, minerals, and bioactive phytochemicals, are now being promoted for dietary supplementation and preventive health care. Modern nutraceutical research highlights its potential in metabolic syndrome, bone health, and women’s health, thereby extending its utility beyond traditional therapeutic contexts.

Given its classical documentation, rich phytochemical profile, validated pharmacological activities, and emerging nutraceutical relevance , L. sativum represents a plant of dual significance- serving both therapeutic and nutritional domains. In this context, the present dossier has been developed to provide a comprehensive, balanced and evidence-based profile of L. sativum, bringing together classical references and contemporary scientific evidence on its pharmacognostic identity, phytochemistry, traditional uses, pharmacological activities, clinical evidence, safety evaluation, and regulatory aspects. The dossier seeks to facilitate informed scientific and regulatory assessment of Chandrasura and to support its quality, rational use and appropriate regulatory oversight.

CHANDRASURA SAFETY DOSSIER Background Lepidium sativum Linn., commonly known as Chandrasura/ Candrasura or Garden Cress, is an annual herb belonging to the Brassicaceae family. It is a plant of significant therapeutic and economic importance, cultivated for its uses in both industry and in individual households, particularly valued for its seeds, leaves, and roots. However, the plant is cultivated mainly for its seed part. Its sprouts, known for their spicy taste, are a popular addition to salads and sandwiches and are considered as a valuable nutritional supplement. Chandrasura holds a prominent place in Indian traditional systems of medicine such as Ayurveda, Unani, and Siddha.

Traditionally, Chandrasura has been utilized for its therapeutic efficacy in managing a diverse range of conditions, including asthma, dysentery, rheumatism, and menstrual disorders. It is especially valued as a galactagogue (a substance that promotes breast milk production) and a general health tonic. The seeds are specifically used for ailments such as coughs, sprains (as poultices), leprosy, various skin diseases, splenomegaly, dyspepsia, lumbago, leucorrhoea, scurvy, and seminal weakness.

The primary purpose of the Safety Dossier of Chandrasura is to compile evidence-based data, presenting a comprehensive account of its historical background, along with preclinical and clinical evaluations related to its safety and efficacy to substantiate the classical therapeutic uses of Chandrasura . The dossier on Chandrasura is prepared, mainly due to rising scientific interest in its therapeutic applications, its significant pharmacological potential, and the growing demand for its uses in traditional medicine, functional foods and phytopharmaceuticals.

Lepidium sativum Linn., commonly known as Chandrasura , garden cress, or Asaliyo , is a therapeutically and nutritionally valuable plant. Its phytochemical composition and reported pharmacological activities have contributed to increasing scientific interest in its potential applications in modern phytomedicine, thereby linking traditional medicinal knowledge with contemporary pharmacological research. It is well recognized in Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and other traditional systems of medicine for its diverse therapeutic applications. Classical texts also describe its inclusion in Paushtik yoga (nutritive formulations) and its role as a Balvardhak (strength-promoting agent))[1], emphasizing its enduring relevance in health and nutrition.

The origin of Chandrasura is believed to be in Ethiopia, where it is locally known as Shifu.[2] Interestingly, Chandrasura is not mentioned in classical Ayurveda treatises like the Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita , and Ashtanga Hridaya , suggesting its introduction into Ayurveda practice occurred in later periods. Its earliest known reference appears around the 12th century in the Shodhala Nighantu, where it was referred to as Asalima or Darakrsna. [3] Acharya Bhavamishra is known for incorporating several foreign plants into Ayurveda literature, and Chandrasura (Chandrika) is among them, recommending it specifically for the treatment of Firanga Roga (~Syphilis). Its seeds were also included in complex Ayurveda formulations such as Chaturbeeja. The therapeutic significance of Chandrasura seeds for Hikka (hiccups) is also documented. [4] A notable historical reference from Bṛhadyogataraṅgi (16th-17th centuries) identifies L. sativum as Ahittha, noting its use as horse fodder- consistent with ethnobotanical evidence of garden cress as forage for livestock. [5] Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu further supports this, citing its diuretic effect in animals.

From the 16th century, the plant became widely known as Chandrasura, while internationally it is called as Garden Cress (English).[4,6] In Unani medicine, it is valued as a diuretic, aperient, demulcent, and aphrodisiac, traditionally used for inflammation, splenic disorders, chest congestion, bronchitis, rheumatism, muscular pain, and to enhance cognition. [7]

L. sativum is a hardy and fast-growing plant requiring minimal care. It can be sown directly in the field after winter frosts or year-round in temperate climates. [8] For a continuous supply of fresh, tender shoots and leaves, sowing should be repeated every 10 to 20 days. Germination typically occurs within 4 to 6 days, and young leaves are ready for harvest within 2 to 3 weeks. [9] It is commonly cultivated during the Rabi season (November to April) and thrives even in low-fertility soils with adequate water retention. The plant’s rapid growth allows for harvesting within the same month of sowing, with potential yields of up to 6 tonnes per hectare. [10] It is extensively cultivated either for their edible foliage (as vegetables) or for the extraction of oil from their seeds. It is recognized as an important plant both in European and Indian dietary traditions, often used as a pot herb. [11] Previously, its seeds were imported into Bombay in significant quantities from Persia, underscoring their value in trade and traditional medicine. [12] Chandrasura is a versatile and historically significant herb with a rich background in traditional medicine and a growing profile in modern scientific research, supporting its therapeutic potential and continued relevance.

Global Demand and Market Potential CHANDRASURA SAFETY DOSSIER L. sativum demonstrates strong global demand potential driven by its diverse uses in traditional medicine, nutraceutical, phytopharmaceutical, agriculture, and functional-food sectors. Seeds of L. sativum are reported as a rich source of protein and dietary fiber, suitable for incorporation into soups, salads, and functional beverages. [13,14] The seeds are also a valuable source of mucilage with gelling, binding, and disintegrating properties, making them suitable for pharmaceutical and food formulations.

Commercially, the plant is available as whole or ground seeds (for food and traditional medicine such as Ayurveda and Unani), seed oil (used in cosmeceuticals and supplements), sprouts or microgreens (fresh produce), and mucilage or extracts (ingredient markets). [15,16,17] Garden cress is recognized as a natural multivitamin rich in essential minerals and vitamins; therefore, it holds significant market potential in the growing global trend toward plant-based and sustainable diets.

Garden cress oil market alone was valued at approximately USD 517.6 million in 2024, with a projected CAGR of 7.8% between 2025 and 2033, expected to reach USD 1.02 billion by 2033, reflecting its steady expansion into nutraceutical and cosmetic segments.[18] Price intelligence data reveal a wide global price range for garden cress seed, from USD 1.3 to 19.6/kg during 2023–2024, largely due to fragmented supply chains and varying quality tiers.[19] Emerging innovations, such as probiotic- enriched garden cress products, highlight the growing potential of functional foods in high- value niche markets. Innovative approaches such as probiotic fortification with Bifidobacterium bifidum expand its role in the functional food industry.[20] Market applications of garden cress extend across multiple domains (1) Nutraceuticals and supplements (capsules, oils, and powders) for glycaemic control, antioxidant support, and iron/omega-3 fortification, supported by preclinical and clinical evidence;.[21] (2) Functional foods, including Halim laddoos, fortified bakery products, beverage premixes, and fresh sprouts/microgreens;.[22] (3) Pharmaceutical and phytopharmaceutical ingredients, such as mucilage as a clean-label excipient and polyphenol-rich extracts for advanced formulations;.[23](4) Cosmetics/ cosmeceuticals, where the seed oil’s antioxidant profile contributes to anti-aging and skin-barrier protection..[24] Geographically, L. sativum is cultivated across South Asia, West Asia, and parts of Africa, with India recognized as a major exporter under the trade name ‘Halim’.[25] Trade records highlight India as a key source of garden cress seed for multiple international markets, although bulk commodity prices typically remain at the lower end of the value spectrum. Demand centres for L. sativum span North America, Europe, and MENA, primarily for nutraceutical and cosmeceutical applications, while functional food adoption remains strongest in traditional- use regions such as India and the Middle East.. [26] Pricing ranges from single-digit USD/kg for bulk commodity seed to double-digit USD/ kg or higher for premium retail packs, certified organic products, and processed derivatives such as extracts or oil- reflecting added value from processing and quality assurance.[27] Competitive differentiation in L. sativum based products can be achieved through standardized active constituents, solvent-free extraction, clean-label excipients, organic certification, and comprehensive safety and efficacy data aligned with regulatory frameworks. It is now widely distributed primarily as a salad crop across Asia as well as in Africa, Europe, North America, and South America.[32,33] It is cultivated extensively across India as per classical Ayurvedic texts.[1,4] In India, it is cultivated on a commercial scale in specific regions, notably in western and south region, primarily for seed production.[32] Cultivation: Chandrasura is a hardy and fast-growing plant cultivated throughout India, Europe, United States, England, France, Asia, etc. All parts are of commercial value, but it is cultivated throughout the world mainly for its seeds and leaves. It can be sown directly in the field after the winter frosts, or year-round in temperate climates.[34] To ensure a continuous supply of fresh, tender shoots and leaves for consumption particularly for salads- sowing should be repeated every 10 to 20 days. Older leaves from early sowings tend to become tough and are no longer suitable for use. Germination typically occurs within 4 to 6 days after sowing, depending on the season.[35] The young leaves are ready to harvest within 2 to 3 weeks. Standard spacing involves keeping 15 to 20 cm between rows. In summer, irrigation is essential, as the shallow-rooted seedlings are prone to drying out quickly. Due to its rapid growth, harvesting can begin within the same month of sowing. It is typically cultivated during the Rabi season (a winter cropping season, typically from November to April). The seeds are sown by broadcasting over a well-prepared field. The crop can also be grown successfully in low-fertility soils with adequate water-retention capacity. Prior to sowing, the field is ploughed 3 to 4 times to achieve proper soil tilth. A seed rate of 8 to 10 kg per hectare is generally recommended. One or two irrigations during the growth period significantly enhance crop establishment and yield.[36] CHANDRASURA SAFETY DOSSIER

The regulatory status of L. sativum varies across jurisdictions, reflecting its extensive traditional use and emerging relevance in modern phytomedicine. In India, a complete monograph is available in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API), Part I, Volume I, under the title Candraśūra (Lepidium sativum Linn.) seeds.[6] This monograph specifies diagnostic parameters for identity (macroscopic and microscopic characters), purity criteria (limits for foreign matter, total ash, acid-insoluble ash, water-soluble and alcohol-soluble extractives), along with therapeutic references and recommended dose. The plant is also widely recognized in Unani medicine (commonly referred to as Habb-ul-Rashaad or Tukhm-i-Halun), and has been cited as an ingredient of compound formulations such as Sharbat Fawlad , a traditional remedy for Faqr al-Dam (anaemia), as documented in the Hippocratic Journal of Unani Medicine issued by the Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine, Ministry of Ayush, Govt. of India.[62] Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and associated rules regulate Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani (ASU) drugs.[63] The plant is also documented in the National Formulary of Unani Medicine and listed in several Ayurveda formulations. [64] In addition, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) recognizes Chandrasura seeds as a food and nutraceutical ingredient under the FSSAI Nutraceuticals and Health Supplements Regulations, 2016, particularly as a source of natural iron and galactagogue formulations, label dose 3–6 g/ day for seed powder and pregnancy caution required.[65] References to the mucilage of L. sativum are noted in European scientific literature for its potential utility as a pharmaceutical excipient, owing to its favourable physicochemical properties. In the WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, L. sativum is not specifically represented, although WHO recognizes its traditional use within broader frameworks of herbal medicines.

The regulatory assessment identifies the root of the Lepidium meyenii as the primary part of possible concern due to its phytochemical composition, specifically the presence of imidazole alkaloids.[70] Internationally, no official documentation for L. sativum exists in The British Pharmacopoeia (BP , 2025 edition), The European Pharmacopoeia, or The Pharmacopoeia of the People’s Republic of China (ChP). Thus, despite extensive documentation in traditional medicine and scientific literature at both national and international levels, L. sativum currently lacks harmonized international pharmacopoeial standards beyond the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India.

Safety Profile of the Plant, including concerns raised on safety L. sativum is generally regarded as safe when consumed in traditional dietary amounts and has a long history of use without major safety concerns. The seeds are rich in nutrients, mucilage, and bioactive compounds, which contribute to their therapeutic and nutritional benefits. Toxicological studies in experimental animals have demonstrated a wide margin of safety, with no significant adverse effects observed at low to moderate dietary doses.

Excessive administration at very high dose through oral route and in dietary feed has been associated with adverse changes in some preclinical experimental studies; however, no clinical studies have reported such toxicity in humans. Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic interactions are reported by Al-Jenoobi and Co-workers (Studies are listed under ‘Non-clinical Pharmacokinetic/ Toxicokinetic studies and Herb–Drug interactions’ section) and postulated that most likely mechanism is interactions with drugs metabolizing cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes but there was lack of experimental data to support these claims.

Furthermore, no international pharmacopoeial or regulatory monographs, including those of the World Health Organization (WHO), European Medicines Agency (EMA), or United States Pharmacopeia (USP), have raised safety concerns regarding the use of L. sativum. The plant is not listed as a restricted or prohibited substance in any major regulatory framework.

In India, it is officially recognized in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India under the name Chandrasura , with defined identity, purity, and quality standards, indicating regulatory acceptance of its safety within traditional therapeutic ranges.[6] The absence of safety warnings in authoritative international monographs suggests that L. sativum is generally considered safe when used in accordance with established traditional practices and recommended dosages.

Nevertheless, as with many herbal substances, the lack of comprehensive global monographs highlights the need for continued pharmacovigilance and well-designed clinical studies to confirm its long-term safety, especially in vulnerable populations and in the context of poly-pharmacy.

Non-Clinical Pharmacokinetic/Toxicokinetic studies and Herb-Drug Interactions Co-administration of Lepidium sativum (garden cress) seeds with conventional pharmaceuticals in animal models produces variable, drug-specific pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions, primarily involving changes in gastrointestinal absorption and systemic exposure, though mechanistic conclusions regarding Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme modulation remain largely speculative. Although L. sativum generally increases systemic exposure and delays elimination of drugs such as cyclosporine, theophylline, phenytoin, and gliclazide, it markedly reduces the oral bioavailability and absorption of sildenafil and accelerates carbamazepine absorption without significantly affecting its overall exposure. However, the clinical relevance of these findings remains uncertain because the evidence is derived with considerable variation in doses and methods of administration. Many studies also used seed powder mixed with feed, making the actual dose consumed difficult to quantify, and many lacked an appropriate L. sativum-alone group or direct mechanistic investigations.

Co-administration also mildly enhances the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel. While in vitro findings indicate moderate, non-dose-dependent inhibition of hepatic CYP2D mRNA expression and metabolic activity, the clinical relevance of CYP isoenzyme or P-glycoprotein modulation by L. sativum remains uncertain and lacks direct experimental validation. Thus, the observed pharmacokinetic changes may be attributable primarily to altered gastrointestinal absorption or plasma protein displacement or elimination rather than established modulation of drug- metabolizing enzymes or transporters because reported studies did not directly investigate these mechanisms.

Co-administration of L. sativum with clopidogrel did not significantly alter core pharmacokinetic exposure parameters, but mildly enhanced the bleeding time. Blood glucose levels were then assessed at multiple time points. Pharmacokinetic analysis showed that, compared to gliclazide alone, co-administra- tion with L. sativum increased the bioavail- ability of gliclazide;

Cmax (8714.9 to 11185.8 ng/mL), (AUC0–t: 29538.3 to 50160.7 ng/mL x h), AUC0–∞ (29826 to 51210.4 ng/mL x h) and T1/2 (3.90 to 6.2 h), decrease in Kel (0.187 to 0.171 h-1) while no change in Tmax. Author reported that, L. sativum alone reduced blood glucose levels by 15.9%, while gliclazide alone produced a 30% reduc- tion. Co-admin- istration of L. sativum with gliclazide resulted in a greater reduc- tion of blood glucose level by 40.5% in diabetic rats.

Although the authors reported a synergistic effect of L. sativum on the glucose-lowering action of gliclazide, careful examina- tion of the data suggests that this effect may not be statistically significant. Plasma concentrations of gliclazide were increased in the presence of L. sativum; however, this did not translate into a significant enhancement of glu- cose-lowering effect of gliclazide.

Although gliclazide is primarily metabolized by CYP2C9 and the authors postulated that the increased bioavailability may be due to CYP2C9 inhibition, this postulation remains speculative as this mechanism is not support- ed by any experimental data and not any known effects that L. sativum inhibits CYP2C9.

However, the inhibitory effect was not dose dependent and appears plateauing at 75 mg/kg.

Even at the highest dose, the inhibitory effects on CYP2D was moderate as we see 80% of the dextromethorphan is still getting metabolized. Therefore, it is inferred that, interaction is unlikely to be clinically significant or associated with drug–drug interactions involving CYP2D substrates.

5. Al-Mohizea et al. (2015) [77] Healthy male beagle dogs (Animal numbers not mentioned) Non-balanced crossover design Interacting drug: Sildenafil Phase I: Dogs received a single oral dose of Sildenafil tablet (100 mg/kg). Blood samples were collected at predetermined time over 24-hour period.

Phase II: After a one-week washout, dogs received L. sativum seeds (7.5 g) mixed with food (30 g) twice daily for eight days. On day 8, sildenafil tablet was re-administered 15 min later after the last L. sativum dose, and blood samples collected at the same time points. Compared with Sildenafil administerd alone, co-administration of Sildenafil with L. sativum resulted into significant decrease Cmax (844 to 508.5 ng/ml), AUC0–∞ (7544 to 3664 ng h/ml, by 51%), non-significant decrease in Tmax (2.38 to 2.25 h) and elimination rate constant Kel (0.182 to 0.177 h-1), while non-significant increase in T1/2 (3.85 to 3.92 h) indicating impaired absorption and oral bioavailability of sildenafil with minimal effects on its elimination kinetics.

Author postulated that L. sativum reduces sildenafil absorption likely via CYP3A modulation or enhanced first-pass metabolism, however this proposed mechanism is speculative as no experimental evidence was provided to substantiate this hypothesis. Limitation: Administration of L. sativum seed powder through feed makes it difficult to determine the precise dose consumed per animal, potentially leading to variability in dosing and pharmacokinetic outcomes.

No explanation was provided for seemingly contradictory results. Also, the doses of L. sativum used for dog studies was way more than used for rodents and rabbits and no justification was provided. In the absence of In vitro data evaluating the effects of L. sativum on drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters, such as CYP450 enzymes and P-glycoprotein, it is not possible to establish a definitive mechanism underlying these pharmacokinetic interactions. Non clinical Toxicology Acute toxicity studies: The available acute oral toxicity studies consistently indicate that Lepidium sativum (L. sativum) seeds and their extracts generally possess a wide acute safety margin, although toxicity varies according to the preparation and dose. The ethanol extract exhibited an LD₅₀ >5000 mg/kg in Wistar rats with only mild, transient symptoms (e.g., lethargy, salivation), and no mortality. The seed powder, tested up to 5 g/kg in rats, also showed no toxic effects or organ damage, classifying it as practically non-toxic. Methanolic, aqueous, acetone and ethyl acetate seed extracts also demonstrated relatively high LD₅₀ values ranging from approximately 5625 to 9000 mg/ kg in mice. The fixed seed oil, demonstrated an LD₅₀ of 2818.32 mg/kg, places the substance in GHS Category 5 and WHO Toxicity Class III classification. Similarly, solid lipid nanoparticles of the extract showed no adverse effects up to tested dose of 400 mg/kg, while the extract alone had an LD₅₀ >5000 mg/kg in mice. Overall, L. sativum seeds and their extracts are considered safe at therapeutic doses, with toxicity mainly observed at very high concentrations. Acute oral toxicity studies of various L. sativum seeds, their tested extracts and oil are practically non-toxic or low toxicity profile following single-dose oral administration in experimental animals, supporting a relatively favourable acute safety profile at therapeutic dose.

Sub-acute toxicity studies: The toxicity profile and physiological effects of L. sativum have been extensively evaluated in various animal models, using different dosage forms such as various extracts of seed powder, seed fixed oil, extract-loaded nanoparticles and at different dose levels. Collectively, reported studies have demonstrated that the safety profile of L. sativum is influenced by the dose, formulation, and duration of administration. From a safety perspective, L. sativum appears generally safe at low to moderate doses and with short-term use across various forms- fixed oil, aqueous or ethanolic or methanolic or acetone or ethyl acetate extracts. Multiple sub-acute toxicity studies in rats and mice demonstrated that lower or moderate doses did not cause significant changes in body weight, organ histology, haematology, or biochemical markers, supporting a favorable safety profile.

However, repeated administration at higher doses was associated with formulation-dependent adverse effects. For example, fixed oil at 564 mg/kg and ethanolic seed extract at doses ≥500 mg/ kg produced hepatic changes, while the ethyl acetate extract at 563 mg/kg resulted in dose- dependent haematological and biochemical alterations. These findings suggest that the potential for organ adverse changes increases with increasing exposure for longer duration and may vary according to the phytochemical composition of the preparation.

In contrast, aqueous, methanolic, and acetone extracts of L. sativum seeds, as well as the ethanolic extract-loaded nanoparticle formulation, were generally well tolerated at the doses investigated, without significant alterations in organ weights, biochemical parameters, or histopathological findings. The fixed oil was well tolerated at 141 and 282 mg/kg but produced hepatic and renal changes at 564 mg/kg, supporting a proposed NOAEL of 282 mg/kg for repeated administration in rats. Overall, these findings support the relative safety of L. sativum at appropriate doses but indicate the need for caution with prolonged administration or higher exposures, particularly with concentrated preparations. Furthermore, the available studies did not comprehensively assess oxidative-stress-related biomarkers; therefore, the absence of reported oxidative changes should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that L. sativum does not induce oxidative stress in target organs during repeated administration.

Repeated oral administration of L. sativum seed fixed oil was well tolerated at lower and mid-dose levels, whereas prolonged exposure or higher doses may pose potential health concerns. Based on the available evidence, the No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) for the fixed oil is inferred to be 282 mg/kg in albino rats on repeated administration.

Extracts of L. sativum are widely characterized for their diverse phytoconstituents and represent the most common form used in food supplements globally. Accordingly, for safety evaluation and related studies, greater emphasis is placed on the raw seed powder and its aqueous or alcoholic extracts. Generally, in global market people use raw powder or extract whereas some of the specific countries like Ethiopia, seed oil is used as part of cooking.

Sub-acute toxicity studies- Repeated dosing in dietary feed: Multiple in vivo toxicity studies evaluating the sub-chronic and repeated-dose dietary administration of L. sativum seed powder consistently demonstrate a highly favorable and non-toxic safety profile at moderate dietary inclusion levels. The L. sativum is well tolerated, exhibiting no mortality or overt signs of clinical toxicity when administered within established safe limits. Dietary inclusion ranging from 1.0% to 10% (w/w) does not negatively impact normal development, as evidenced by stable weekly food consumption, mean body weight, and final body weight gain.

Furthermore, supplementation maintains healthy physiological functions without adversely affecting glycaemic status, haematological indices, or hepatic and pancreatic oxidative stress markers. CHANDRASURA SAFETY DOSSIER

Comprehensive macroscopic and microscopic histological evaluations confirm that the seed powder does not induce structural abnormalities or tissue lesions in vital organs, and absolute and relative organ weights remain comparable to healthy controls. Although minor, dose-dependent, and sex-specific increases in certain liver enzymes (such as ALP and SGOT) have been observed at higher dietary concentrations (5.0% and 10.0%), these variations remain within normal physiological boundaries and complete absence of corresponding histopathological alterations indicates a safe, adaptive response rather than overt hepatotoxicity.

Duration of study: 6 weeks The results of this study demonstrate that dietary administration of L. sativum seed powder at 2% (w/w) was non-toxic and well tolerated, while higher dose inclusion levels (10% and 50% w/w of the diet) were associated with dose-dependent toxicity, manifested as entero-hepato-nephrotoxici- ty and macrocytic hypochromic anaemia in Wistar albino rats. Notably, the 50% dietary inclusion level was found to be lethal over a 6-week exposure period. Overall, these results suggest a clear dose-dependent safety profile, with low-level dietary inclusion (2% w/w) appearing safe.

It was inferred that, NOAEL for L. sativum seed powder administered through the diet is 2% w/w on repeated administration. Considering an average daily food intake of approximately 15 g for a 200 g adult rat, a 2% dietary inclusion corresponds to an intake of about 300 mg/day, which is equivalent to approximately 1500 mg/kg/day. This dose may be regarded as safe under the study conditions.

Reproductive toxicology studies The reported evidence suggests that Lepidium sativum demonstrate a highly favorable reproductive safety profile across multiple animal models, with no evidence of systemic toxicity or detrimental physiological effects at moderate therapeutic doses. It is observed that, Lepidium sativum may exert several beneficial physiological and reproductive effects in experimental animals without producing overt toxicity at the doses and durations investigated. Aqueous extracts administered at 100 – 600 mg/kg doses exhibited no adverse effects on fertility, sperm quality, or hormonal balance in male rodents. Conversely, these doses have been shown to increase serum testosterone and, at higher doses, enhanced sexual behaviour and reproductive parameters, while the 60-day study in rats showed no adverse effects on spermatogenesis, sperm quality, testicular oxidative-stress markers, or general health. Dietary supplementation with whole L. sativum seed powder in rabbits improved reproductive performance, litter size, milk production, milk composition, lipid profile, renal function, and antioxidant status. Similarly, L. sativum sprout powder improved hepatic lipid metabolism without affecting growth or liver weight, while seed oil enhanced post-thaw sperm motility, viability, morphology, acrosomal integrity, and mitochondrial function in boars. In female mammals, seed supplementation is safely tolerated with no observable maternal, lactational, or fertility-related toxicities. Summary of pre-clinical studies of plant In vitro studies The safety and therapeutic potential of L. sativum extracts and derivatives has been extensively investigated in normal cell lines and cancer-associated and disease-related cell lines. Importantly, normal human skin fibroblasts L929 cell lines, as well as non-cancerous TM3 Leydig, and splenic cells, showed greater tolerance to L. sativum, particularly at low-to-moderate concentrations. In some cases, these preparations exerted protective or bio-stimulatory effects, with substantial toxicity observed only at markedly higher doses. Further, Lepidium sativum (garden cress) demonstrates pronounced, dose- and time-dependent anticancer activity, acting primarily through apoptosis induction and cell viability suppression. Cytotoxic potency varies significantly by extraction method and delivery system: organic solvent fractions (methanolic, methylene chloride, n-hexane) and nanoparticle formulations exhibit superior anti-proliferative effects with lower IC50 values (frequently under 50 µg/mL) compared to crude aqueous or polysaccharide extracts.

This differential response suggests a degree of selectivity toward cancer cells over normal cells and supports the potential for a favourable therapeutic window, with effective cytotoxicity against cancer cell lines while maintaining relative safety in non-cancerous tissues at appropriate therapeutic doses.

In vivo experimental efficacy studies Chandrasura (L. sativum), exhibits a wide range of pharmacological effects validated in various animal models. Its seed extracts, particularly in ethanolic, methanolic, and aqueous forms, have demonstrated hepatoprotective and nephroprotective properties in chemically-induced relevant animal models. L. sativum exerts dose-dependent, multi-targeted protective effects mainly through its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and cytoprotective properties. It shows notable anti-diabetic effects, effectively lowering blood glucose, enhancing insulin sensitivity, and protecting against diabetic complications, including nephropathy, testicular damage, and pancreatic dysfunction. Chandrasura has also been shown to regulate lipid metabolism, alleviate metabolic syndrome, and reduce hyperlipidaemia, likely through antioxidant and insulin-signalling pathways.

In reproductive health, it improves fertility in PCOS and hyperprolactinemia models, restoring hormone balance and reproductive organ health. Its gastrointestinal benefits include anti-diarrheal and laxative effects via modulation of intestinal motility. L. sativum (Chandrasura) exhibits potent anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties through the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α), prostaglandin synthesis, fibroblast activity, and oxidative stress.

The seed oil modulated immune mediators by enhancing omega-3 fatty acids and suppressing lymphocyte proliferation and macrophage activation without impairing immune defence. Chandrasura also showed therapeutic potential in various disease models: it reduced colon cancer incidence by promoting apoptosis and minimizing genotoxicity; accelerated diabetic wound healing via collagen synthesis and antioxidant activity; mitigated Alzheimer’s-related neurodegeneration by normalizing biomarkers (Aβ, tau, AchE), reducing oxidative and inflammatory damage, and enhancing cognition; suppressed thyroid hormone levels and modulated thyroid histology; dose- dependent bronchoprotection in asthma models; and enhanced immune function through dose- dependent stimulation of both humoral and cell-mediated immunity. Furthermore, it showed significant anti-parasitic activity against Trypanosoma species, attenuated osteoporosis by modulating bone remodelling markers (RANKL/OPG), and accelerated fracture healing through enhanced callus formation and bone repair. Overall, the multifaceted pharmacological profile of Chandrasura underscores its potential as a versatile therapeutic agent in traditional and modern medicine.

II GOKSHURA SAFETY DOSSIER Prologue Medicinal plants continue to play an important role in healthcare systems worldwide, providing valuable resources for traditional medicine, modern phytopharmaceuticals, and nutraceutical products. Their increasing use and commercialization have underscored the need for robust scientific evidence to establish their quality, safety, efficacy, and rational utilization. Regulatory authorities internationally are placing greater emphasis on systematic, evidence- based safety evaluation of botanical medicines, particularly those with extensive traditional use and widespread availability as herbal medicines and dietary supplements.

Tribulus terrestris L., known as Gokshura in Ayurveda, is an important medicinal plant widely recognized and used in several traditional systems of medicine, including Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy. It is also included in various national and international pharmacopoeias and is used as an ingredient in numerous classical, proprietary, and contemporary botanical preparations. Traditionally, Gokshura has been used for a range of health conditions, particularly those involving the urinary and reproductive systems, as well as metabolic and musculoskeletal disorders. In recent years, the international use of Tribulus terrestris L. has expanded beyond traditional applications, with preparations containing the plant increasingly marketed for sexual health, energy, physical performance, sports performance etc.

The phytochemical profile of Tribulus terrestris L. is complex and includes saponins, sapogenins, flavonoids, alkaloids, phenolic compounds, and other secondary metabolites. The composition and concentration of these constituents may vary according to geographical origin, developmental stage, extraction methods, and processing etc. Such variability is an important consideration when interpreting pharmacological and toxicological findings and assessing the safety of commercially available preparations. Accordingly, the safety profile of Tribulus terrestris cannot be considered independent of the identity and quality of the plant material or preparation, including the plant part used, method of processing or extraction, composition, dose, and duration of exposure.

The extensive traditional use and growing global commercialization of Tribulus terrestris L. have generated considerable scientific and regulatory interest in its safety. Available experimental and clinical evidence provides important information regarding its tolerability under defined conditions of use; however, isolated adverse events and evolving regulatory assessments highlight the need for continued critical evaluation. Safety findings should be interpreted in relation to the specific plant material or preparation, dose, duration of exposure, population studied, route of administration, and quality characteristics of the product, rather than being generalized across all preparations of Tribulus terrestris L.

III GOKSHURA SAFETY DOSSIER The present Gokshura Safety Dossier has been developed as a comprehensive, evidence-based scientific resource for the objective assessment of the safety profile of Tribulus terrestris L. It integrates evidence from traditional medical literature, phytochemistry, pharmacological investigations, clinical studies, pharmacovigilance reports, and relevant national and international regulatory publications. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluating the strength of the available evidences, identifying reported safety concerns, and distinguishing established findings from areas where evidence remains limited or inconclusive.

The dossier is intended to support informed scientific and regulatory decision- making by providing a balanced assessment of the available evidences on the safety of Tribulus terrestris L. It is designed to serve as a reference for regulatory authorities, researchers, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and stakeholders involved in the development, manufacture, evaluation, regulation, and responsible use of medicinal and botanical products.

Through the systematic compilation and critical appraisal of available evidence, this dossier seeks to contribute to the scientifically sound evaluation of Gokshura and to promote its quality, safety, rational use, and appropriate regulatory oversight in the interest of public health.

The aim is to provide a consolidated and scientifically validated reference that underscores the herb’s pharmacological efficacy and safety at therapeutic doses. It has become more imperative in light of emerging regulatory deliberations at the international level, particularly the recent recommendations of the Heads of European Food Safety Agencies (HoA) Working Group on Food Supplements, June 2024, Tribulus terrestris L. (Gokshura) has been identified as a botanical ingredient requiring prioritized safety evaluation under the ‘ Article 8 Procedure’ of Regulation (EC) No. 1925/2006. The report highlights potential risks associated with the concentrated intake of certain herbal substances through food supplements and recommends harmonised regulation within the European Union. The Tribulus terrestris L., based on clinical observations, have possibly been linked with neuronal, hepatic and renal toxicity. It further stated that animal studies have also reported toxic effects, such as in vitro cytotoxicity, genotoxicity and estrogenicity. From these observations, it becomes imperative to comprehensively document the traditional knowledge base, therapeutic rationale, and scientific evidence supporting its safety and efficacy.

Introduction Gokshura (Tribulus terrestris L.) is one of the most frequently employed medicinal plants across Indian traditional systems of medicine, including Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Sowa Rigpa and Homoeopathy. The plant, botanically classified as Tribulus terrestris L., is a prostrate to procumbent herb with yellow flowers and schizocarpic spiny fruits, predominantly found in arid climates and sandy soils. The roots and fruits of the plant are traditionally used in the Ayush systems for a broad range of health conditions, especially those related to the urinary, reproductive, and metabolic systems. The pharmacological potential of Tribulus terrestris L. is attributed to its rich phytochemical profile, comprising steroidal saponins (furostanol and spirostanol types), flavonoids, tannins, alkaloids (like diosgenin, hecogenin, and gitogenin), terpenoids, phenolic acids, and potassium nitrate. These bioactive constituents are considered responsible for the plant’s diverse therapeutic properties. The fruits of Tribulus terrestris L. are extensively used not only in Ayurvedic Medicine in India but also in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and ethnomedicine in regions like Bulgaria. The herb is documented in the Japanese Pharmacopoeia, Korean Pharmacopoeia and Pharmacopoeia of China and described as a valuable drug in the ancient Shen-Nong Pharmacopoeia of China.

GOKSHURA SAFETY DOSSIER Pharmacologically, Gokshura exhibits a wide spectrum of validated actions, including diuretic, nephroprotective, aphrodisiac, antiurolithic, immunomodulatory, antidiabetic, absorption-enhancing, hypolipidemic, cardio-tonic, central nervous system supportive, hepato-protective, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antispasmodic, anticancer, antibacterial, anthelmintic, larvicidal, and anti-carcinogenic activities.

These properties are well-documented through classical Ayurvedic texts as well as modern scientific literature. Global Demand and Market Potentials The herb Tribulus terrestris L. has demonstrated rising global demand and significant commercial value, driven by expanding international markets for standardized botanical extracts. In international trade, Tribulus terrestris extracts are classified under HS Code 13021919 - a residual tariff classification covering unspecified vegetable saps and extracts. Under this broader export line, standardized extracts specifically derived from Tribulus terrestris represent an active commercial commodity, recording multi-million dollar annual trade across active global supply chains.(1) Technical Specifications General Information Scientific name: Tribulus terrestris L.

Animals were closely monitored for 14 days for signs of toxicity, changes in behaviour, and body weight.

oral toxicity study, female Wistar rats were administered a single dose of Tribulus terrestris L. methanolic extract of fruit at 2000 mg/kg, in accordance with OECD Guideline 425. Animals were closely monitored for 14 days for signs of toxicity, changes in behaviour, and body weight.

On the 14th day, blood samples and organs were collected. The haematological analysis revealed no significant changes in key parameters, including haemoglobin, RBC, WBC, haematocrit, MCV, MCH, MCHC, and differential counts, when compared to the control group. A significant increase in platelet count was observed (p<0.001). Biochemical tests revealed a substantial reduction in cholesterol levels and a rise in alkaline phosphatase, which may suggest mild biliary involvement. However, other liver and kidney function markers, including ALT , AST , creatinine, urea, protein, and albumin, remained within normal ranges, indicating that organ functions were preserved.

Histopathological examination of the heart, liver, and kidney revealed normal tissue architecture, with no signs of necrosis, inflammation, or structural damage, confirming that biochemical changes in alkaline phosphatase are not linked to hepatic changes and the absence of gross toxic effects at the tested dose level (22) Abbas et al. (2022) also evaluated the safety profile in an acute oral toxicity study of Tribulus terrestris L., conducted in accordance with OECD Guideline 423 . Wistar rats were administered the TT 100% methanolic extract of fruits at limit doses of 2000 mg/kg and 3000 mg/kg body weight, orally. Animals were observed at intervals of 1, 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours’ post-administration for any signs of toxicity, followed by daily monitoring over a 14-day period. No mortality, behavioural changes, or signs of toxicity were observed.

Body weight gain remained unaffected, and organ weights (liver, kidney, and heart) were within normal ranges. Gross necropsy and histopathological examination revealed no treatment-related pathological alterations. Based on the absence of adverse effects or mortality, the LD₅₀ of the methanolic extract of Tribulus terrestris L. was estimated to be ≥3000 mg/kg, indicating that the methanolic extract of Tribulus terrestris L. is non-toxic at the tested doses under acute exposure conditions in Wistar rats.(23) Kaushik et al (2019) performed an acute oral toxicity study on an aqueous extract of the dried and matured fruits of Tribulus terrestris L. The extract was prepared using cold maceration at 23.5 °C for 19.5 hours with a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:12 (w/v), followed by filtration and lyophilization. A single dose of 2000 mg/kg body weight was administered orally to Wistar rats (5 males and 5 females), following the OECD Guideline 423. Animals were observed for 14 days for clinical signs, mortality, and body weight changes. No toxicological effects or gross pathological alterations were observed, indicating that the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of the aqueous extract of fruits of Tribulus terrestris L. is greater than 2000 mg/kg body weight, orally in albino rats.(24) Sub-acute toxicity (28 day) Several subacute toxicity studies have been conducted to evaluate the safety of Tribulus terrestris L. extracts in animal models.

Tribulus terrestris L. increased the serum testosterone in rats. There were no differences in the other semen characteristics, relative weight of organs and serum levels of urea, creatinine, alanine and aspartate transaminase, gamma glutamyl transferase, cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone. No adverse effects were observed at 100 mg/kg dose level of Tribulus terrestris L., indicating a favourable safety profile of the plant extract. However, the extract of Tribulus terrestris L. has notable effects on male reproductive hormones in rats. (25) There are gross limitations of this study, e.g. the exclusive use of male rats, which prevents assessment of potential sex-based variations in toxicity; absence of multiple dose levels required to determine the dose-response relationship, etc.

Due to these limitations and not following OECD guidelines, this study was excluded from the safety evaluation of Tribulus terrestris L. Across all the subacute toxicity studies in rats (28-day repeated oral administration), key assessment parameters included behavioural observations, body and organ weight monitoring, haematological profiles, biochemical markers and histopathological analysis of vital organs. The collective findings demonstrate that Tribulus terrestris L., administered at doses ranging up to 1000 mg/ kg bw/day orally, did not produce any major toxic or adverse effects in rats, thereby

All studies incorporated different extracts of Tribulus terrestris L.; methanolic and ethanolic extracts were used to obtain a broad spectrum of active compounds for comprehensive toxicity evaluation, while aqueous extracts were chosen to reflect traditional preparation methods. Genotoxicity Studies Abudayyak et al. (2014 ) carried out the in vitro genotoxicity study of water, methanol, and chloroform extracts of whole plants of Tribulus terrestris L. In the study, the genotoxic potential of Tribulus terrestris L. was characterized by two separate in vitro assays (Comet and Ames genotoxicity assays). The results obtained from the Comet assay showed that DNA damage was not induced in NRK-52E cells exposed to extracts of Tribulus terrestris L. for 24 h.

Significant differences were not found in tail intensity in NRK-52E cells treated with the plant extracts compared with the control group. The methanol and chloroform extracts of Tribulus terrestris L. showed no evidence of mutagenic activity against S. typhimurium TA98 and TA100 at concentrations of 30, 60, 300, 600, 1200, and 2400 µg /mL in the Ames assay. However, the water extracts of Tribulus terrestris L. at the concentrations above 300 µg /mL were mutagenic to the TA100 strain when metabolically activated and induced frame shift mutations.(26) Qari et al. (2019) conducted an in vitro study to assess the genotoxic potential of aqueous extracts of Tribulus terrestris L. fruits using both the comet assay and cytogenetic techniques on cultured human peripheral blood lymphocytes. Lymphocytes were treated with varying concentrations (10, 20, 40, and 80 mg/L) of the extract for 24 hours. Low concentrations (10–20 mg/L) showed no statistically significant differences from the control group, and higher concentrations (40– 80 mg/L) induced marked genotoxic effects.

After 45 days, female rabbits from both groups were mated with control male rabbits.(34) The number and survivability of offspring were estimated. The experiment was continued with female newborns (F1 female generation), two new groups were formed, control and experimental, of 7 females each to the origin from the mothers’ generation. Tribulus terrestris L. and Hepatic Safety Pre-clinical studies Tribulus terrestris L. has diversely opposite effect on the liver ranging from liver protection to liver injury in animals grazing on the plant. There are reports from South Africa that sheep and goat grazing on Tribulus terrestris L. suffered from multiple symptoms like severe inflammation of ears, eyelids due to increased photosensitivity to UV light, jaundice and discomfort. This is attributed to very high doses of steroidal saponins and other toxins of the plant. Aslani et al. (2003), reproduced this phenomenon experimentally. They collected aerial part of the plant, while in the flowering to seeding stage from the Sabzevar district of Khorasan Province, air dried and stored for use in the experiment. Seven native goats (1- to 2-year-old) were fed ad libitum by Tribulus terrestris L. for 8 weeks (56 days). Water was freely available to animals during the study.

The study by Bourke CA (2012) explored a potential mechanism underlying motor neuron disease (MND) in sheep associated with the ingestion of Tribulus terrestris L. This chronic and geographically restricted disorder is characterized by astrocyte degeneration in the central nervous system without significant neuronal loss. The study hypothesized that a combination of dietary molybdenum (Mo) deficiency and ingestion of xanthosine, a purine nucleoside present in Tribulus terrestris L., could lead to the condition. To test this, eight Border Leicester crossbred sheep were fed Mo- deficient lucerne chaff and sodium tungstate (a Mo antagonist) for three weeks to induce Mo deficiency, followed by xanthosine administration (25 mg/kg/day) mixed into the feed for 18 weeks. After the feeding period, the sheep were returned to pasture and monitored for 42 months. Two sheep (25%) developed clinical signs of chronic and irreversible MND at 30–30.5 months, including asymmetrical hindlimb paresis, decreased muscle tone, neurogenic atrophy, and reluctance to walk.

Histopathological examination of all animals revealed varying degrees of astrocyte degeneration in several specific brainstem and spinal cord nuclei, mirroring the lesions seen in field cases of Tribulus-associated MND. The findings suggest that in purine-salvaging

Controlled clinical studies and uncontrolled case reports to address the safety concerns An initial title and abstract screening of available literature on the clinical efficacy of Tribulus terrestris L. was performed, during which irrelevant or non-clinical studies were excluded. This systematic screening process yielded 28 eligible clinical studies for detailed analysis. (6) use in prostate-related disorders. This domain-wise classification enabled a structured synthesis of evidence regarding the safety and diverse clinical applications of Tribulus terrestris L. across multiple patho- physiological conditions. GOKSHURA SAFETY DOSSIER A comprehensive review of the toxicological and clinical safety profile of Tribulus terrestris L. reveals a consistently favourable safety margin across various experimental and clinical settings. The dossier evaluated 271 studies, including pre-clinical pharmacological studies, toxicological assessments and human clinical trials. In the cytotoxicity studies, four key in vitro experiments demonstrated that Tribulus terrestris L. extracts exhibit minimal to no cytotoxicity at therapeutic concentrations (10–25 µg/mL). Mild to moderate cytotoxic effects were observed only at significantly higher concentrations (≥50 µg/mL), indicating a clear dose-dependent safety threshold. These findings support the conclusion that Tribulus terrestris L. is safe at recommended dosages.

Acute toxicity was assessed in three major studies using rat models. In all cases, even high doses up to 3000 mg/kg of methanolic or aqueous extracts did not cause mortality or behavioural abnormalities. The estimated LD₅₀ values were above 2000–3000 mg/kg, which aligns with the classification of the plant extract as having low acute toxicity potential. Subacute toxicity studies were also conducted over 28- day periods using oral administration in rats at doses ranging from 500 to 1000 mg/kg. These studies showed no adverse effects on haematological, biochemical, or histopathological parameters, particularly in organs like the liver, kidneys, and heart. These findings reinforce the historical usage of Tribulus terrestris L. and confirm its safe profile even with repeated dosing.

These findings reinforce the historical usage of Tribulus terrestris L. and confirm its safe profile even with repeated dosing.

Regarding genotoxicity and mutagenicity, two detailed in vitro studies found no genotoxic effects at therapeutic concentrations (10–20 mg/L). Genotoxic alterations such as chromosomal stickiness or micronuclei formation were observed only at much higher doses (40–80 mg/L). Considering the doses recommended to use as a food supplement and low systemic exposure due to high metabolism, it is highly unlikely that some of the in vitro genotoxic effects will translate in vivo, and sub- acute toxicity studies underlined the safety of the herb. The absence of genotoxicity at clinical levels strengthens the plant’s candidacy for safe therapeutic use. The pre-clinical efficacy segment reviewed 167 studies, with 25 focusing specifically on reproductive health.

These studies, conducted on rodents, rabbits, and other models, found Tribulus terrestris L. to be non-toxic during pregnancy and beneficial for both male and female reproductive function. No adverse maternal or developmental outcomes were observed, and significant improvements in hormone levels, follicular development, and sperm parameters were noted, with no histological evidence of damage to reproductive tissues.

In the clinical domain, 28 human studies were analysed. In male reproductive health (8 studies), standardised extracts of Tribulus terrestris L. (750–1500 mg/day) consistently improved sperm count, motility, erectile function, and testosterone levels and all these effects were within normal physiological limits.

These studies reported no major adverse events, with only minor complaints such as transient gastrointestinal discomfort in isolated cases. For female reproductive health, six clinical trials suggest the possible use of Tribulus terrestris L. in managing conditions like PCOS, hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), and menstrual irregularities at doses ranged from 280 mg/day to 750 mg/ day. Most subjects experienced significant improvements in hormonal profiles and quality-of-life scores, and only mild side effects such as flu-like symptoms, with no serious toxicity.

GOKSHURA SAFETY DOSSIER In the management of metabolic disorders, three trials demonstrated statistically significant reductions in fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, and lipid parameters following Tribulus terrestris L. administration, with no adverse reactions. Similarly, in trials related to athletic performance and endurance (seven studies), the herb was found to be safe, without signs of hepatotoxicity or renal stress. Two additional studies were conducted on healthy volunteers, and two on prostate-related disorders, and all these studies further prove the tolerability and safety of Tribulus terrestris L.

The safety of Tribulus terrestris L. as an ingredient in food supplements remains a subject of regulatory scrutiny and scientific debate. A critical analysis of the summarized reports and evaluations from national and international authorities (DTU, AECOSAN, Zespół do spraw suplementów diety, RASFF) reveals a complex safety profile, influenced by dosage, plant part used, preparation method, and saponin content. An extensive evaluation of the published literature, focused on the safety of the herb, is undertaken in this document, which support that the use of Tribulus terrestris L. as food supplement at recommended doses and free from any adulteration is safe without any major side effects.
